headline: Madras HC refuses to dismiss Bangladesh's plea to cancel 'Tangail Sarees of Bengal' GI
reference: West Bengal State Handloom Weavers Co-operative Society Ltd vs Deputy Commissioner Tangail, (GI) A No. 1 of 2026 in OP(GI) No. 1 of 2025, Madras High Court, 2026:MHC:4695 (GI)
summary_points: Issue: whether the Tangail Deputy Commissioner's Section 27 GI Act petition to cancel the 'Tangail Sarees of Bengal' GI can be rejected at the threshold.
Held: Application seeking dismissal rejected; the petitioner's locus and status as 'person aggrieved' need a full enquiry or trial.
Court noted the petitioner could seek its own GI in India, which the existing registration would obstruct, so the petition is maintainable at this stage.
Delay plea rejected: petitioner said it learnt of the GI only in February 2024 and filed in December 2024; journal advertisement did not bar relief.
Trade mark rulings cited by the applicant were held inapplicable to the GI Act's Sections 27, 31, 58 and Rule 65; no costs ordered.
who_is_affected: GI registrants, weaver and producer bodies, and IP counsel dealing with GI registrations and foreign challenges to them.
action_required: GI holders should review the registration basis and be ready to defend against rectification petitions, including from foreign parties; read the full order for the reasoning on Section 27 and Rule 65.

social.linkedin:
The Madras High Court has refused to summarily dismiss a petition by the Deputy Commissioner, Tangail (Bangladesh) seeking cancellation or rectification of the GI registered for 'Tangail Sarees of Bengal'.

The West Bengal State Handloom Weavers Co-operative Society argued that the petitioner is not a 'person aggrieved' under Section 27 of the GI Act, that Rule 65 offers a remedy before the Registrar, and that the petition is delayed.

Justice P.B. Balaji dismissed the application. Key takeaways:

- Locus and 'person aggrieved' status need a full enquiry, not threshold rejection.
- The petitioner could seek its own GI in India, which the existing registration would obstruct.
- The petitioner said it learnt of the GI only in February 2024 and filed in December 2024, so no fatal delay was found.
- Trade mark precedents cited by the applicant were held inapplicable.

The petition now proceeds to a full trial. This matters for GI holders and IP practitioners, as it signals that foreign parties may challenge Indian GI registrations.

Please verify with the official judgment before relying on this summary.
